nameStory: The twenty-spotted lady beetle gets its straightforward name from the numerous dark spots scattered across its pale wing covers. While many people expect lady beetles to have just a few spots, this species breaks the mold with its busy polka-dot pattern that can actually vary from 15 to 20+ spots per individual.
description: The twenty-spotted lady beetle is a small, pale yellow to cream-colored lady beetle decorated with many black spots across its wing covers. Unlike the classic red lady beetles most people know, this species has a softer, more subdued appearance. It's quite small, typically measuring about 3-4 millimeters long—roughly the size of a small peppercorn. What makes this lady beetle special is that it feeds on fungus and mildew rather than aphids like most of its relatives.

idTips.label: Spot Pattern
idTips.description: Look for 15-20 small black spots scattered across pale yellow to cream wing covers—the spots feel smooth to the touch and are clearly defined against the light background

idTips.label: Body Color
idTips.description: The overall color is pale yellow to cream, sometimes appearing almost white in bright sunlight—much lighter than the bright reds and oranges of most lady beetles

idTips.label: Size
idTips.description: Very small at 3-4mm long, about the size of a small peppercorn—you can barely feel its weight when it crawls on your hand

idTips.label: Head Markings
idTips.description: The head often has dark markings or spots and appears proportionally large compared to the small body

idTips.label: Behavior
idTips.description: Often found crawling on leaves covered with powdery mildew or other fungal growth, moving slowly as it feeds on the fuzzy fungal patches

idTips.label: Body Shape
idTips.description: Typical dome-shaped lady beetle form but feels delicate and lightweight when handled, with a smooth, slightly glossy surface

habitat: Look for twenty-spotted lady beetles in gardens, forest edges, and anywhere plants show signs of powdery mildew or other fungal diseases. They're particularly common on trees and shrubs with fungal growth, including ornamental plants, fruit trees, and native understory vegetation. You'll often find them in partially shaded areas where humidity allows fungal diseases to thrive on plant surfaces.

seasonality.spring: Adults emerge and become active, seeking out early fungal growth on new plant growth. This is when you're most likely to spot them moving between plants.
seasonality.summer: Peak activity period when fungal diseases are common on plants during humid weather. Adults are feeding actively and may be found mating.
seasonality.fall: Still active through early fall, taking advantage of late-season fungal growth. Adults begin seeking overwintering sites in leaf litter.
seasonality.winter: Adults hibernate under bark, in leaf litter, or other protected spots. Not visible unless you disturb their hiding places during warm spells.

funFact: While most lady beetles are fierce predators that can devour 50+ aphids per day, the twenty-spotted lady beetle is actually a gentle vegetarian that specializes in eating fungus—making it nature's tiny cleanup crew that helps keep plants healthy by removing harmful mildew and mold!
confusionNotes: Most commonly confused with other pale lady beetles, but the twenty-spotted stands out with its unusually high number of spots. Remember: "Twenty spots, feeds on rot"—if you see lots of spots on a pale lady beetle near fungal growth, you've found your species. Other pale lady beetles typically have far fewer, larger spots.
contextualKnowledge: Many people assume all lady beetles are beneficial predators, but the twenty-spotted lady beetle represents a fascinating exception as a fungus-eater. This dietary difference means it's not competing with other lady beetles for food—instead, it's filling a completely different ecological niche as nature's fungal management specialist.
compareHints: As the only Psyllobora species commonly found in New England, the twenty-spotted lady beetle is unique among local lady beetles for its pale color and numerous spots. Most other regional lady beetles are red or orange with fewer, larger spots and feed on insects rather than fungus. The combination of cream color, many small spots, and association with fungal growth makes this species unmistakable once you know what to look for.
